strengths: A well-designed multi-teacher distillation framework that unifies complementary 2D signals—language-aligned (SigLIP2), generalist visual (DINOv3), and object-aware (PE-Spatial)—into a shared, versatile 3DGS scene encoder.

Outstanding data efficiency: demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot semantic and instance segmentation while using significantly fewer training scenes (8.32× and 39.9× less than point-cloud pretraining baselines).

Comprehensive and diverse evaluations across multiple modalities and tasks, including open-vocabulary 3D semantic/instance segmentation, visual question answering (VLM grounding), and traditional linear/decoder probing.
The 'render-and-distill' online adaptation strategy is highly practical, successfully removing the need for massive offline storage and precomputation of 3D pseudo-labels on novel datasets.
Strong technical execution including novel 3DGS-aware augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold) and standardization techniques (PHI-S) to balance multi-teacher optimization.
weaknesses: Model complexity and latency: Table 10 shows Chorus has the largest parameter count (131.3M) and the slowest inference time per scene (0.70s) compared to baselines like SceneSplat (91.7M, 0.65s) and Sonata (108.5M, 0.49s).

Slight ambiguity on Point Cloud cross-modality: It should be clearer in the main text that the point cloud benchmark uses a separately trained model variant ('using only Gaussians’ centers, colors, estimated normals as inputs') rather than the exact same 3DGS model weights performing zero-shot transfer.
Key mathematical details regarding the proposed 3DGS-aware augmentations and teacher-specific contrastive losses are deferred entirely to the supplementary material.

The evaluation is restricted to indoor environments (ScanNet, ScanNet++, MP3D, InteriorGS); how the framework generalizes to larger-scale outdoor scenes where 3DGS characteristics differ remains unaddressed.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated formulation that integrates complementary signals (language-aligned, generalist visual, and object-aware) from multiple 2D foundation models into a unified 3DGS representation.

Very strong empirical results across a diverse set of tasks, including zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic/instance segmentation, 3D visual question answering, and standard semantic probing/finetuning on point cloud benchmarks.

The proposed render-and-distill adaptation is highly efficient and practical, eliminating the need for costly offline 3D pseudo-label preprocessing and significantly reducing storage requirements (from ~1 TB to 8 GB on InteriorGS).

Excellent data-efficiency and cross-representation transferability, where a point-cloud compatible variant of Chorus achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised baselines while using up to 39.9× fewer pretraining scenes.
Sound design choices and thorough ablations, such as using PHI-S teacher standardization, staged training strategies, and introducing novel 3DGS-aware augmentations.
weaknesses: The model size (131.3M parameters) and average inference time per scene (0.7s) are slightly higher than some prior baselines (like Mosaic3D or Sonata), indicating a trade-off between holistic capability and computational overhead.

The 3DGS-specific augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) are described only qualitatively in Section 3.4; including their basic mathematical formulations in the main text would make the methodology more self-contained.

The optimal training recipe relies on a staged training schedule (e.g., introducing the PE-Spatial teacher in the second half). A discussion on the sensitivity of this schedule and whether further scheduling exploration was conducted would strengthen the work.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple downstream tasks including zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, 3D visual question answering (VQA), and point cloud transfer tasks.

High data-efficiency, showing strong transfer capability and competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Sonata) while using significantly fewer training scenes (8.3x to 39.9x less data).

The proposed 'render-and-distill' online adaptation pipeline is a clever addition that avoids heavy offline 3D pseudo-label preprocessing, which greatly improves storage efficiency (from ~1 TB to 8 GB).

Well-motivated, 3DGS-aware augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) that respect the rendering mechanics and optimization dynamics of 3D Gaussian Splatting, showing improvements over naive point-cloud style augmentations.
weaknesses: The framework exhibits high complexity and is largely an assembly of existing components (such as SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial, PHI-S normalization, and Sonata's 3D backbone). The fundamental architectural and algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited.
Increased computational overhead, where Chorus has the largest model size (131.3M parameters) and slowest inference time (0.7s per scene) among the compared approaches in Table 10.

The optimization process appears highly sensitive, requiring a complex staged pretraining schedule (introducing the PE-Spatial teacher only in the second half of training) to prevent over-anchoring to local features, which might limit its robustness and generalizability to new dataset configurations.

The explanation and justification of why a 3DGS-trained encoder transfers so well to point clouds remains somewhat speculative. It is not fully clear if the robustness is a direct consequence of the 3DGS representation or simply because the multi-teacher setup provides superior regularized signals.

strengths: Holistic and Novel Pretraining Paradigm: Distilling complementary representations (language-aligned, generalist visual features, and object-aware spatial cues) from heterogeneous 2D models (SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial) to pretrain a general feed-forward 3DGS encoder is a well-designed and novel exploration for 3D scene representations.

Impressive Cross-Modality Transfer: The finding that pretraining on 3DGS parameter space generalizes effectively to traditional point cloud benchmarks (achieving competitive performance to Sonata while using 39.9x fewer scenes) is a highly interesting and valuable scientific contribution.

Practical Render-and-Distill Adaptation: The online render-and-distill adaptation strategy significantly reduces out-of-distribution finetuning costs, eliminating the massive 1TB+ storage requirement for precomputing 3D pseudo-labels and enabling lightweight optimization using only 2D rendered views.

Excellent Experimental Evaluation: The paper is backed by extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks (ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, InteriorGS) on multiple challenging tasks (semantic/instance segmentation, visual question answering, probing, and data-efficiency studies).

High-Quality Visualization: The PCA visualization, UMAP analysis, and VQA qualitative results effectively demonstrate the semantic consistency and geometry awareness of the learned embeddings compared to existing baselines.
weaknesses: Increased Computational Overhead for Initial Pretraining: While the online adaptation is highly efficient, the initial offline multi-teacher pretraining requires running inference on multiple large-scale 2D models (SigLIP2-so400m, DINOv3-ViT-L, PE-Spatial-L) and lifting them to 3D, which is computationally expensive.

Higher Latency and Parameter Footprint: As shown in Table 12, Chorus has a larger parameter size (131.3M) and a slightly slower inference time (0.70s per scene) compared to existing baselines like SceneSplat (91.7M, 0.65s) and Sonata (108.5M, 0.49s). While still highly practical, this is a trade-off worth highlighting.

Main-text Self-Containment on Augmentations: The mathematical formulations and detailed implementations of the two proposed 3DGS-aware augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) are relegated to the supplementary material. Moving a brief summary of these formulations to the main text would improve self-containment.

strengths: The proposed multi-teacher pretraining framework for 3DGS is highly novel, successfully distilling language-aligned, generalist visual, and object-aware 2D priors into a single general-purpose 3DGS scene encoder.

The paper presents extensive and thorough evaluations across multiple challenging benchmarks and tasks, including zero-shot semantic/instance segmentation, probing, and LLM-based 3D visual question answering, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.

The proposed render-and-distill online adaptation pipeline is extremely practical, significantly reducing the storage and computation footprint for out-of-domain finetuning by avoiding heavy 3D feature precomputation.

The introduces two well-motivated, 3DGS-aware data augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) with sound theoretical justifications regarding appearance preservation and coarse-to-fine optimization dynamics.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality visualizations, clear figures, and a comprehensive supplementary section detailing dataset processing (such as the InteriorGS dataset splits) and pipeline algorithms.
weaknesses: Although online adaptation is lightweight, the initial pretraining stage still suffers from high computational and storage overhead due to the requirement of precomputing and lifting dense 2D teacher features (e.g., requiring ~1TB of storage for 800 scenes).
Inference runtime (0.7s per scene) is slightly slower than some of the simpler point-cloud and 3DGS baselines, which might present a minor bottleneck for real-time mobile and robotic systems.
The 3D encoder is inherently bounded by the performance, domain limits, and potential biases of the chosen 2D teacher models (SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial).

strengths: A well-designed multi-teacher distillation framework that successfully unifies complementary semantic, visual, and spatial cues (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial) into a single general-purpose 3DGS scene encoder.
The proposed 'render-and-distill' online adaptation is highly practical, allowing out-of-domain fine-tuning directly on rendered images and avoiding costly 3D feature preprocessing.

Specifically designed 3DGS-aware augmentations (rendering-equivalent perturbation and immature-manifold perturbation) are theoretically grounded and shown to be superior to naive point-cloud augmentations.

Impressive empirical performance across a wide array of benchmarks (ScanNet, ScanNet++, InteriorGS) and tasks, including semantic/instance segmentation, zero-shot open-vocabulary tasks, and 3D visual question answering.
The finding that 3DGS pretraining transfers extremely well to point-cloud tasks (outperforming state-of-the-art point-cloud SSL methods with much less data) is highly interesting and well-validated.
weaknesses: The model size (131.3M parameters) and inference time (0.70s per scene) are slightly higher than previous 3DGS/point-cloud encoders, which might affect highly resource-constrained deployment scenarios.

Pretraining still requires precomputing and storing heavy 3D pseudo-labels offline (up to 1TB for 800 scenes), although this is mitigated during the downstream adaptation stage by the online render-and-distill approach.
